note: Second constitutional spine. Architecture and developing doctrine only — not detailed election or redistricting legislation. No invented statistics. Research precedes policy drafting.
role_in_philosophy: Constitutional Capitalism cannot return economic power to the people while leaving political power concentrated in legislatures, parties, donors, governors, and courts.

foundational_principle.text: No branch, party, officeholder, donor class, or temporary majority should be able to convert electoral victory into permanent control of the republic.

trust_doctrine.text: Political authority is held in trust, never owned. No officeholder, legislature, party, court, executive, donor, or institution may lawfully convert temporary public authority into permanent control. Power must remain divided, visible, reviewable, locally rooted where possible, and continuously returnable to the people.

anti_entrenchment_doctrine.text: No temporary majority may use public power principally to make itself harder to remove, harder to investigate, or less accountable to the electorate.

party_principle.text: A political party may support a candidate, but it should not own the office, the district, or the voter.

distributed_government_objective.text: Strong enough to protect rights and perform necessary public functions, but too divided, transparent, and accountable for any temporary faction to capture permanently.

hierarchy_rule: Each level receives only the power necessary to perform functions that lower levels cannot perform effectively or constitutionally. Constitutional rights remain the floor beneath every level.
problem_machinery: party leaders choosing candidates before voters do
officeholders using public visibility to build private wealth
governors and legislative supermajorities reshaping courts and election rules
legislatures stripping authority from local governments
donors and lobbyists gaining more access than ordinary citizens
procedural rules preventing bills from receiving open debate
unified party control eroding meaningful separation of powers

pillars.title: Community-rooted representation
pillars.summary: Candidates must build support inside the community they will represent; parties organize ideas but should not be private gatekeepers controlling public offices.
principles: nonpartisan or broadly accessible preliminary elections
limits on formal party control over ballot access
election methods that reward broader community support

pillars.title: End self-interested redistricting
pillars.summary: Districts should reflect people and communities rather than predetermined electoral outcomes. Goal is not manufactured equal seat shares for parties.
standards: redistricting body institutionally separated from current legislators
respect for genuine communities of interest
limits on splitting cities, counties, and neighborhoods
judicial review under clear state or federal standards
prohibition on using incumbent addresses or election forecasts when constructing initial maps

pillars.title: Prevent legislative supremacy
pillars.summary: A legislature is one institution temporarily entrusted with legislative power — not the people themselves.
prohibited_patterns: seize routine authority from municipalities after disliking a local decision
alter election rules solely to entrench its majority
abolish independent oversight bodies investigating lawmakers
weaken courts in retaliation for adverse decisions
delegate excessive emergency power and then selectively reclaim it
prevent voter-approved laws from taking effect without an extraordinary process
manipulate legislative procedure to prevent recorded votes
use appropriations to punish constitutionally independent institutions

pillars.title: Structural independence under unified party control
pillars.summary: Checks must not depend only on party competition. No political coalition should control legislation, enforcement, adjudication, election administration, ethics enforcement, and district design through the same uninterrupted chain of loyalty.
safeguards: staggered terms for important oversight bodies
fixed procedures for filling judicial vacancies
supermajority requirements for altering election administration
bipartisan or multipartisan approval for certain watchdog appointments
guaranteed minority-party subpoena and hearing rights
judicial review protected from retaliatory budget manipulation
public standing to challenge violations of structural constitutional rules
mandatory sunset review of emergency powers

pillars.title: Legislative procedure belongs to the public
pillars.summary: Political power hidden in procedure must become visible, reviewable, and accountable.

pillars.title: Public office is not a private wealth engine
pillars.summary: Holding office should be public service — not privileged access to investment information, contracts, lobbying relationships, or future employment. Term limits alone are insufficient; transparency and anti-monetization rules are essential.

pillars.title: Community representation in legislative institutions
pillars.summary: A citizen should know who represents the community, be able to reach that representative, understand how that representative voted, and have a realistic opportunity to replace that representative. No single mechanism declared universally superior before testing.

pillars.title: Local home rule with constitutional floors
pillars.summary: Presumption of local authority over genuinely local matters; state preemption requires publicly stated statewide necessity. Local majorities may not violate individual rights.

pillars.title: Citizen constitutional backstop
pillars.summary: Representative government remains primary; citizens retain peaceful corrective mechanisms with safeguards against billionaire domination and deceptive ballot language.

pillars.title: Courts independent without judicial supremacy
pillars.summary: Legislatures write laws; executives implement; courts interpret constitutional boundaries; citizens remain ultimate sovereign through lawful constitutional processes.

questions.text: Who asked for it?
Who wrote it?
Who benefits?
Who pays?
Which level of government gains power?
Which level loses power?
What rights are affected?
How will success be measured?
When will the law be reviewed?
How can it be repealed or corrected?

democracy_test.title: Constitutional Capitalism Democracy Test
democracy_test.purpose: Screen political-structure reforms before acceptance into the framework.

questions.text: Does it make political power more returnable to the people?
Does it reduce the ability of a temporary majority to entrench itself?
Does it keep parties as associations serving voters rather than owners of offices?
Does redistricting reflect communities rather than predetermined outcomes?
Does it preserve meaningful separation of powers under unified party control?
Does legislative procedure remain visible and publicly reviewable?
Does it prevent public office from becoming a private wealth engine?
Does it protect local home rule while keeping constitutional rights as a floor?
Does it preserve independent courts without judicial supremacy?
Does it increase ordinary citizens’ realistic ability to contest, understand, and correct government?

legislative_procedure_requirements: bills published for a minimum public-review period
identification of sponsors and material authors
publicly available fiscal and local-impact statements
emergency procedures limited to actual emergencies
success_measures: citizens can identify and contact their representatives
unified government does not eliminate oversight
ordinary citizens can realistically run and win
